content:
Threading is done by associating messages with each other according to information in their email headers, specifically, the "Message-ID" and "References" lines. You can view these normally hidden headers by pressing <Ctrl+U> when a message is selected. The lines are generated by the sender's email program when they respond to a message, in which case those references are carried over in their reply.

The chain can be broken when the sender's program neglects to properly create those reference lines, or if the sender adds to the topic by creating a fresh message rather then responding to an existing one. There may be other places the chain can be broken. Point being, it's somewhat fragile.

So, no, not a bug, that's just the way it works (or sometimes doesn't work.) It's not repairable, but you might be able to see a particular topic all together by use of Thunderbird's various searches and filters. Which one is most effective would depend on the topic itself, like if they all have the same subject line.

content:
It's difficult to find the cause of a problem which happens once in awhile. To evoke a new bug the issue must be reproducible. By default Thunderbird proceeds with an automatic session restore, and I have not yet seen a failure of this feature. The session data are stored in the Thunderbird profile in a file named session.json which is actualised on each closure of the app. There is a second file named session.json.backup which is a copy of a previous session.json file. So if your problem happens again you can open the Thunderbird profile folder, delete the actual session.json file and rename session.json.backup file in session.json before restarting Thunderbird.

To navigate to the profile folder go to Help > Troubleshooting Information > Profile Folder > Open Folder, then quit Thunderbird before doing the above instructions.

Hello there Vickie



Good news: the connection and ports for IMAP and SMTP are working, as shown by the green ticks during setup. However, your email provider is blocking the login on your new laptop because most providers no longer accept a standard password for new setups in desktop email apps.


To fix this in the Thunderbird desktop app on your new Asus Zenbook, please follow these steps:


1. In the setup wizard, click Manual config and change the Authentication method from Normal password to OAuth2 for both Incoming (IMAP) and Outgoing (SMTP), then click Re-test and Done.

2. If the account is already added in the Thunderbird desktop app, go to Account Settings (via the menu icon ≡ in the top right) and change the Authentication method to OAuth2 under both Server Settings (IMAP) and Outgoing Server (SMTP).

3. Restart Thunderbird. A browser pop-up will appear asking you to log in and grant Thunderbird permission.


If your email provider (such as iCloud or a local internet provider) does not support OAuth2, log in to your webmail in your browser, generate a dedicated App Password in your security settings, and use that password in Thunderbird instead.

content:
Hello there Schlief.incorporated


The error "Server gmail.com has disconnected" is not a Thunderbird bug and does not require a patch.

It is triggered by Gmail’s daily IMAP bandwidth and connection limits after transferring tens of thousands of emails. Because it has been stuck since last night, your account has likely hit Gmail's 24-hour data cap.



Please follow these steps to resume the migration:

1. Wait 24 hours: Close Thunderbird completely for 24 hours so Google automatically lifts the temporary IMAP rate limit on your account.

2. Lower cached connections: In Thunderbird, go to Account Settings > Server Settings > Advanced... and reduce Maximum number of server connections to cache from 5 to 1 or 2.

3. Exclude "All Mail" (if migrating from Gmail): In Gmail webmail, go to Settings > See all settings > Labels and uncheck Show in IMAP for All Mail to prevent duplicate downloads.

4. Transfer in batches: Disable computer sleep mode and migrate one or two folders at a time instead of the entire mailbox at once. Once the 24-hour cooldown expires and the connection limit is lowered, the transfer should resume normally.


Tip : One quick tip regarding VPNs: If you are using a VPN on your computer, try pausing it temporarily while migrating your emails.

Gmail’s IMAP servers are notoriously strict with shared VPN IP addresses and can drop the connection immediately if the VPN briefly hiccups or switches servers during a large transfer.


Grab a coffee, close Thunderbird for the night, and let Google’s 24-hour timer do its thing. Let me know tomorrow how the transfer goes once you lower the connection limit—I’ll be right here if you need a hand.

.
